items.title: How can empowering leadership foster employee–AI collaboration? A multilevel analysis of AI trust and psychological safety
items.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the workplace underscores the urgent need to understand how employees collaborate effectively with AI systems. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigates the impact of empowering leadership on employee–AI collaboration. Furthermore, we examine the mediating roles of psychological safety and AI trust. Design/methodology/approach To test the research model, we utilized a multilevel design data from 418 employees across 103 teams in AI-integrated organizations in Vietnam. Findings Our findings indicate that empowering leadership is positively related to employee–AI collaboration, with this relationship mediated by both psychological safety and AI trust. Originality/value This study contributes to the leadership and technology management literature by establishing a multilevel link between empowering leadership and employee–AI collaboration. It identifies key mediating mechanisms (AI trust and psychological safety), offering a more integrated understanding of leadership influence in AI-enabled settings. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for practitioners navigating the dynamics of employee–AI collaboration, highlighting the importance of empowering leadership in building AI-ready workforces.

items.title: Human Factors in Brain–Computer Interfaces: Boundaries, Key Issues, and Methodological Approaches
items.abstract: The large-scale, real-world deployment of brain–computer interface (BCI) is confronted with human factors bottlenecks, including reliability and usability. While modern human factors engineering has encompassed domains such as cognitive ergonomics, workload, adaptive automation, and human-in-the-loop systems, its theories and methodologies have historically placed their main emphasis on overt behavior and peripheral physiological measures, rather than on central neural activity as a primary control input. For the emerging interaction paradigm that takes central nervous activity as direct input and emphasizes long-term brain–computer co-adaptation, there remains a shortage of targeted conceptual and methodological frameworks. As a conceptual review, this paper discusses the necessity and disciplinary foundations for developing Human Factors Engineering for BCIs as an emerging interdisciplinary research direction. First, grounded in the defining features of BCI interaction—such as the implicit nature of input and brain–computer co-adaptation—it delineates the research boundaries and summarizes the core research objects as user neurocognitive characteristics, brain–computer collaborative adaptation mechanisms, multimodal feedback regulation, and contextual adaptation patterns. Second, it identifies three core scientific questions: individual differences and dynamic adaptation, human factors optimization and fault tolerance, and contextual generalizability principles, with ethics, privacy, and user rights and interests as an overarching dimension. Furthermore, it constructs a methodological system consisting of multimodal measurement and modeling, closed-loop validation, and multidimensional evaluation, and examines the supporting role of artificial intelligence approaches within this framework. Centered on the collaborative adaptation across neural, cognitive, and system levels, Human Factors Engineering for BCIs represents a deepening of the human-centered design philosophy. It provides theoretical reference for user-friendly BCI design and extends the research boundaries of human factors engineering.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of performing cognitive work that was previously associated primarily with human intellectual ability. Generative AI can now assist with writing, analysis, reasoning, coding, interpretation, and decision support, allowing individuals to produce sophisticated intellectual outputs that may exceed their independently demonstrated understanding. As a result, the quality of human output may become an increasingly incomplete indicator of the cognitive capability genuinely possessed by the human producing it.This conceptual opinion paper proposes Human Genuine Intelligence (HGI) as a framework for examining this emerging distinction. HGI refers to the cognitive capacity that humans genuinely possess, understand, and exercise through question formation, independent reasoning, analytical thinking, evidence evaluation, causal understanding, judgment, and cognitive revision.The paper introduces Borrowed Intelligence (BI) and the Cognitive Dependency Gap (CDG) as conceptual lenses for examining potential mismatches between AI-augmented capability and independently accountable human cognitive capability. Rather than advocating reduced use of AI, it proposes Active Cognitive Augmentation (ACA) as a model for human–AI interaction: THINK → ASK → AUGMENT → CHALLENGE → VERIFY → REVISE → DECIDE WITH WISDOM.The paper further argues that cognitive capability alone is insufficient for navigating increasingly powerful AI systems. HGI therefore needs to be considered alongside Human Wisdom, which provides direction and responsibility, and Cognitive Sovereignty, which concerns the preservation of human agency and authority over consequential goals, values, delegation boundaries, and decisions.The central challenge of the AI age is therefore not to preserve human intelligence by limiting artificial intelligence, but to strengthen human cognition, wisdom, and agency while using increasingly capable machines.

items.abstract: AI incident databases and risk taxonomies are increasingly valuable, but they often answer broad questions about harm, misuse, or system failure rather than the narrower operational question of whether humans remain meaningfully in control of increasingly agentic systems. This paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for analyzing agent-control failures: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. The framework separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. This v1.1 revision updates the paper title to better distinguish the work while preserving the Human in Control project name, the existing Human Control Model, the six-dimension framework, the original version lineage, and the publication record family. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. The prepared local export updates the recoverable v1.0.1 manuscript title and metadata; the prior longer sandbox-only v1.1 manuscript was unavailable. Creator: Human in Control Project. items.title: Human, Organisational, and Navigational Factors in Selected North Sea Ship Collisions: A Qualitative Comparative Case Study
items.abstract: Ship collisions in the North Sea remain a significant maritime safety concern because the region combines merchant traffic, fishing activity, offshore operations, and traffic separation schemes. This study examines five purposively selected North Sea ship collisions occurring between 2010 and 2023 to identify recurring human, organisational, and navigational factors and develop practical lessons for reducing collision risk. A qualitative comparative case-study approach was employed using official Marine Accident Investigation Branch and Dutch Safety Board reports. Documentary analysis and thematic coding covered 22 factors across five cases. The most consistently supported weaknesses concerned lookout and monitoring, situation awareness, risk of collision assessment, and electronic navigational information. Communication, bridge redundancy, and organisational controls also showed deficiencies, although their form and evidential support differed. Evidence concerning fatigue and some organisational explanations was qualified. The cross-case interpretation identified erosion of overlapping safety barriers before impact, while recognising functioning safeguards and limitations in the report evidence. The findings support recommendations for observable watchkeeping standards, effective technology use, bridge-team support, fatigue-aware operations, and organisational verification. These conclusions concern the selected cases and do not establish the frequency or causal strength of the factors across all North Sea collisions.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Financial Advice on Investment Preferences and Risk Perception among Salaried Investors
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to deliver financial information, investment recommendations and portfolio decision support. This study examines the proposed impact of AI-based financial advice on investment preferences and risk perception among salaried investors. The framework treats perceived usefulness, perceived accuracy, trust, personalisation and transparency as dimensions of AI-based financial advice and tests their proposed relationships with investment preference and risk perception. A quantitative cross-sectional design using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire is proposed. For demonstration of the intended empirical reporting format, a synthetic dataset of 450 hypothetical salaried investors was generated and analysed using internal-consistency assessment and regression-style structural estimates. The simulated results indicate positive associations between the five AI-advice attributes and investment preference and negative associations with risk perception. These numerical findings are illustrative only and must not be represented as observations from real respondents. The study contributes a focused framework for future primary research on AI-assisted investment decision-making among salaried investors.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Tools on the Learning Behaviour and Academic Engagement of Generation Z Students
items.abstract: Abstract It is evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) now plays and important role in every students life. It is being adapted progressively becoming an inevitable part of almost every student’s academic performance. The use of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva, and many more AI-based learning platforms support student learning effectively. These tools aid as search engine machines used to extract information. Students often use AI learning based platforms for synthezising challenging concepts, seeking creative assignment ideas. They also use AI tools for taming writing skills and specifically during preparation of their exam preparation. Generation Z, is known to be digitally native so they have grown up in an environment which is highly digital in nature. So they are highly privileged to secure an environment that not only supports but also openly accepts wide usage of AI based technologies. This adoption of AI based technology learning not only designs their day to day living easy, but also supports them in their learning processes. AI tools facilitate learning quicker in less time and features personalised learning. AI based learning tools are easily accessible for students as they are either free of cost or offered to students at lower costs. Although excessive dependence on AI based tools for learning is not fit for students as, it restricts their independent critical thinking blocking their creativity minds and hinders problem-solving abilities. The main purpose of the research paper was to scrutinize the impact of AI tools on the learning behaviour of Gen Z students. The study is an attempt to focus on gauging the frequency with which the Gen Z students use AI learning tools, understanding the purpose of AI usage. An analysis is done through to pivot lenses on the influence of AI based learning on various parameters like learning efficiency, change academic engagement, and the perception of students. It will give a clear picture whether students hold AI based learning as an advantage or a possible limitation when adopted for educational purposes.

items.title: Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach
items.abstract: This record serves as a living document for a 12-session course titled "Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach," delivered at Farhangian University (Tehran, Iran) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The course transforms pre-service social science teachers from passive consumers of curriculum into active "architects of learning environments" through the integration of Generative AI into instructional design. It equips student-teachers with the competencies needed to design, evaluate, and redesign instructional materials that are pedagogically sound, contextually grounded, and resistant to uncritical AI substitution. The course comprises twelve interconnected lesson packages, each containing: (1) a classical instructional design source, summarized as a Persian-language module with theoretical foundations and practical examples; (2) an avant-garde AI-related article exploring emerging research and applications in AI-mediated education; and (3) a structured prompt toolkit enabling student-teachers to co-design instruction with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. The course follows a three-stage progression: • Critical Exploration — using AI to surface the limitations of traditional linear instructional models and to identify their epistemological assumptions; • Co-Design Synthesis — applying the Integrated AI Triad (IAT) framework to co-create lesson plans and redesign passive curriculum units with a focus on authentic, context-anchored learning; • Reflective Validation — documenting design decisions through structured prompts, blind peer adjudication, and reflective journaling. Twelve thematic sessions cover: the foundations of instructional design; learning theories and AI; problem definition; needs assessment; learning outcomes; content redesign; strategies for concepts and procedures; principles and causal relationships; higher-order thinking; assessment design; interactive message design; and reflective synthesis. Course outputs include 29 redesigned lesson plans from three national sociology textbooks (Sociology 1, Sociology 2, and Sociology 3), developed collaboratively by 29 student-teacher teams. All redesigned lessons are released as an open dataset to support reproducible research in AI-mediated instructional design. This record is updated weekly throughout the semester. Each update adds the lesson package corresponding to the current session. The Concept DOI remains constant, ensuring a single persistent link for the entire course.

items.title: Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach
items.abstract: This record serves as a living document for a 12-session course titled "Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach," delivered at Farhangian University (Tehran, Iran) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The course transforms pre-service social science teachers from passive consumers of curriculum into active "architects of learning environments" through the integration of Generative AI into instructional design. It equips student-teachers with the competencies needed to design, evaluate, and redesign instructional materials that are pedagogically sound, contextually grounded, and resistant to uncritical AI substitution. The course comprises twelve interconnected lesson packages, each containing: (1) a classical instructional design source, summarized as a Persian-language module with theoretical foundations and practical examples; (2) an avant-garde AI-related article exploring emerging research and applications in AI-mediated education; and (3) a structured prompt toolkit enabling student-teachers to co-design instruction with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. The course follows a three-stage progression: • Critical Exploration — using AI to surface the limitations of traditional linear instructional models and to identify their epistemological assumptions; • Co-Design Synthesis — applying the Integrated AI Triad (IAT) framework to co-create lesson plans and redesign passive curriculum units with a focus on authentic, context-anchored learning; • Reflective Validation — documenting design decisions through structured prompts, blind peer adjudication, and reflective journaling. Twelve thematic sessions cover: the foundations of instructional design; learning theories and AI; problem definition; needs assessment; learning outcomes; content redesign; strategies for concepts and procedures; principles and causal relationships; higher-order thinking; assessment design; interactive message design; and reflective synthesis. Course outputs include 29 redesigned lesson plans from three national sociology textbooks (Sociology 1, Sociology 2, and Sociology 3), developed collaboratively by 29 student-teacher teams. All redesigned lessons are released as an open dataset to support reproducible research in AI-mediated instructional design. This record is updated weekly throughout the semester. Each update adds the lesson package corresponding to the current session. The Concept DOI remains constant, ensuring a single persistent link for the entire course.

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity has intensified concerns about the opacity of complex models, which undermines stakeholder trust and slows adoption. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses this by producing justifications for model decisions, yet such justifications are typically delivered as raw textual or numerical output that many stakeholders find difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates XAI with advanced data visualization, treating visualization as a first-class layer of the explanation pipeline rather than an afterthought: post-hoc attribution methods supply explanation content, and purpose-designed visual encodings — heatmaps, feature-importance dashboards, and decision-path graphs — supply a cognitively efficient form. Beyond the framework, the paper specifies a standardized, falsifiable evaluation protocol spanning three benchmark domains and seven measurable constructs — explanation satisfaction, objective understanding, decision accuracy, cognitive load, subjective trust, calibrated trust, and decision confidence — with directional hypotheses grounded in perceptual and cognitive-explanation theory. A structured results-reporting design is included to support immediate empirical application. The primary contribution is the framework, the measurement standard, and the evaluation protocol.

items.title: Judgment Formation in AI-Mediated Inquiry: A Preliminary Generative Relational Account
items.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary Generative Relational (GR) account of judgment formation in AI-mediated inquiry. Its analytical object is not judgment in general and not a contest between human and artificial judgment. The paper examines how historically developed capacities for framing, discrimination, confidence calibration, selective reliance, revision, responsibility, and learning are reorganized when artificial intelligence can participate in generating options, reasons, evaluations, recommendations, and polished answers. The starting distinction is between improved task performance and the development of judgment. AI assistance can improve performance while leaving the user poorly calibrated about the quality or provenance of the resulting decision, and algorithmic advice can influence both decisions and confidence in ways conditioned by metacognitive sensitivity. The paper therefore treats judgment formation as a history-bearing, relational process whose relevant unit may be a coupled Human–AI configuration rather than an isolated individual. Subsequent sections examine the AI-mediated judgment environment, calibration and selective reliance, problem salience, aesthetic, normative, practical, and trajectory-sensitive judgment, reflexive effects of present judgment on future judgment conditions, power over judgment criteria, delegation and responsibility, practices for judgment under AI mediation, cultivation and productive cognitive friction, and the assessment of judgment development. The framework does not reserve mature judgment to humans, prescribe a universal decision procedure, or infer judgment quality from answer accuracy alone. Its purpose is to provide a revisable conceptual architecture for studying how judgment can remain calibrated, responsibility-bearing, and developmentally generative as artificial assistance becomes more capable.

items.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
items.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.

items.title: MODERN APPROACHES TO ENHANCING MEDIA LITERACY AND DESIGN SKILLS IN PROFESSIONAL EDUCATION CONTEXTS
items.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of industrial and technical sectors requires professional education institutions to align curriculum design with contemporary digital imperatives. Traditional vocational frameworks often treat media consumption and visual communication as isolated peripheral skills rather than core engineering competencies. This study presents a comprehensive pedagogical framework designed to integrate media literacy, visual design skills, and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools into technical and vocational education and training (TVET). By combining Project-Based Learning (PBL) with digital diagnostic tools and cloud-based collaborative design environments (e.g., Canva, Figma, Adobe Express, Google Workspace), the proposed model fosters critical information evaluation, visual storytelling, and technical documentation proficiency. The article outlines a multi-layered curriculum architecture, systematic assessment matrices, and iterative project workflows structured around real-world technical problems. Empirical implementation models demonstrate that embedding AI-assisted content verification alongside visual design workflows significantly improves vocational students' analytical skills, technical layout quality, algorithmic awareness, and professional digital collaboration, ultimately bridging the gap between academic preparation and modern industry standards.

items.title: More than we can make: generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming
items.abstract: Abstract Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

items.title: Nanotechnology-enabled occupational health and safety as a strategic driver of crisis management: An empirical study of electricity maintenance departments in Baghdad
items.abstract: Occupational health and safety (OHS) has emerged as a strategic organizational function that contributes not only to employee protection but also to organizational resilience and crisis preparedness. Effective communication, meanwhile, plays a vital role in facilitating information exchange, coordination, and decision-making during emergency situations. This study investigates the impact of occupational health and safety on crisis management through the mediating role of effective communication in the Electricity Maintenance Departments of Baghdad, Al-Karkh. A quantitative descriptive–analytical approach is adopted, and data are collected using a structured questionnaire distributed to a comprehensive census sample of 56 managerial and supervisory employees, including department heads, division and unit supervisors, work supervisors, and team leaders. The study examined three principal constructs: occupational health and safety, effective communication, and crisis management. Data are analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics and IBM SPSS Amos through descriptive statistics, reliability and validity assessments, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling (SEM), and mediation analysis. The results confirmed the adequacy and validity of the measurement models and revealed significant positive relationships among the study variables. Occupational health and safety are found to exert a direct positive effect on crisis management, indicating that organizations with stronger safety practices demonstrate greater preparedness, response capability, and recovery effectiveness during crises. Effective communication also showed a significant positive influence on crisis management by enhancing coordination, information credibility, communication speed, flexibility, and feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, occupational health and safety significantly improved effective communication, while mediation analysis confirmed that effective communication partially mediates the relationship between occupational health and safety and crisis management. These findings emphasize the importance of integrating occupational health and safety systems with effective communication strategies to strengthen crisis preparedness, improve organizational resilience, enhance operational continuity, and support effective crisis management in high-risk electricity maintenance environments.

items.title: Negotiating generative AI in online and distance higher education: lecturers' task-selective adoption in Yogyakarta, Indonesia
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how lecturers in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, adopt and negotiate the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic work, focusing on perceived usefulness, task-selective use, ethical ambivalence and institutional readiness. Design/methodology/approach A convergent mixed-methods design combined an online survey of 120 lecturers from public and private universities in Yogyakarta with semi-structured interviews with eight lecturers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and compared across age, academic rank and institution type using the Kruskal–Wallis H test; interview data were analyzed thematically. The strands were merged during interpretation. Findings All respondents (100%, n = 120) agreed that generative AI improves academic efficiency (M = 4.47). However, agreement declined across presentations (56.7%), teaching material preparation (53.3%), disciplinary understanding (51.7%), scholarly articles (48.3%), research (46.7%) and academic books (46.7%), indicating task-selective adoption. None of the task-specific usefulness ratings differed significantly by age or academic rank (all p > 0.05), but perceived training need differed significantly by age and rank, with a large effect for age and a moderate effect for academic rank (both p < 0.001). Institution type was associated with attitudes toward AI for academic books and toward AI possibly replacing lecturers (both p < 0.05). Interviews revealed the same task-selective logic, alongside ethical ambivalence about plagiarism and dependency and a perceived absence of institutional guidance. Research limitations/implications The study used purposive convenience sampling in one Indonesian province, with an unequal public-private institutional ratio, a cross-sectional self-report survey and eight interviews. The findings therefore cannot support causal claims or represent all Indonesian lecturers, higher education institutions, or open and distance learning (ODL) systems. Negotiated professional adoption remains an emergent interpretation that requires further testing. Future research should use multisite, more balanced and longitudinal designs to examine institutional differences and changes in lecturers' AI practices as policies and technologies evolve. Practical implications Universities should issue task-specific policies that distinguish legitimate AI assistance from inappropriate substitution, especially in scholarly writing and research. They should establish authorship-disclosure rules, verification procedures and clear academic-integrity mechanisms. Lecturers need guidance on checking AI-generated content and preserving professional judgment. ODL administrators should provide differentiated training based on seniority and need rather than uniform programs. National bodies should set minimum standards, while institutions should adapt operational policies to their own contexts. Social implications Clear institutional guidance can support responsible generative AI use while protecting academic integrity, professional accountability and trust in higher education. Differentiated training can reduce uneven preparedness across age groups and academic ranks. Transparent rules on authorship, verification and acceptable use may help lecturers and students understand the boundaries between assistance and substitution. These measures can encourage fairer, more consistent and more trustworthy use of generative AI in digitally mediated and open and distance higher education. Originality/value The study proposes negotiated professional adoption as an emergent, contextually grounded conceptual interpretation that extends the Technology Acceptance Model with professional, ethical and institutional dimensions specific to generative AI in open and distance higher education.

items.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical opportunities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the management of vocational education institutions. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence for educational planning, coordination of teachers’ activities, monitoring learners’ performance, analyzing educational outcomes, and supporting management decisions. Particular attention is given to the organizational and pedagogical conditions required for the effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into vocational education management. The study demonstrates that the use of artificial intelligence can contribute to improving the efficiency, timeliness, and data-based nature of management processes. At the same time, pedagogical appropriateness, data security, the development of teachers’ digital competence, and human oversight are identified as important conditions for the responsible and effective use of artificial intelligence.

items.abstract: Abstrak: Kegiatan pengabdian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh rendahnya literasi digital guru sekolah dasar dalam memanfaatkan kecerdasan buatan (AI) sebagai media pembelajaran interaktif, sementara siswa generasi digital cenderung lebih tertarik pada permainan digital dibandingkan metode pembelajaran konvensional. Tujuan pengabdian ini adalah meningkatkan kompetensi guru dalam memanfaatkan Gemini AI untuk merancang game edukasi interaktif serta meningkatkan motivasi dan hasil belajar siswa. Mitra kegiatan adalah 10 guru dan 5 kelas SD Inpres yang berlokasi di kampung Ampas, Provinsi Papua. Metode pelaksanaan meliputi workshop literasi AI, pelatihan desain game edukasi berbasis project-based learning, pendampingan intensif, dan implementasi di kelas dengan evaluasi menggunakan instrumen pretest-posttest sebanyak 15 soal dan angket motivasi belajar sebanyak 20 pernyataan. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan 85% guru mampu memanfaatkan Gemini AI secara mandiri, dihasilkan lima produk game edukasi interaktif, motivasi belajar siswa meningkat 23%, dan hasil belajar siswa meningkat 18% pada materi yang diujikan. Kegiatan ini terbukti efektif meningkatkan literasi digital guru dan menghadirkan pembelajaran yang lebih interaktif, kontekstual, dan menyenangkan.Abstract: This community service program was motivated by the low digital literacy of elementary school teachers in utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) as an interactive learning medium, while digital-native students tend to be more interested in games than conventional learning methods. The program aimed to improve teachers competence in using Gemini AI to design interactive educational games and to increase students learning motivation and outcomes. The partners were ten teachers and five classes at a state elementary school (SD Inpres) located in Kampung Ampas, Papua Province. The method consisted of an AI literacy workshop, project-based training in educational game design, intensive mentoring, and classroom implementation, evaluated using a 15 item pretest-posttest and a 20 staetement learning motivation questionnaire. The results showed that 85% of teachers were able to use Gemini AI independently, five interactive educational games were produced, student learning motivation increased by 23%, and learning outcomes increased by 18% on the tested material. The program proved effective in strengthening teachers digital literacy and creating more interactive, contextual, and enjoyable learning.

items.title: Processes of Patterning: AI, Literacy, and the Epistemological Challenge
items.abstract: Abstract This article develops a conceptual analysis of what occurs when central dimensions of literacy are outsourced to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems. Classical conceptions of literacy, sociocultural theories of mediated learning, and postdigital perspectives on knowledge practices, provide the theoretical foundation to further the argument that contemporary AI tools reshape the developmental processes through which judgement, independent thinking, and internal structures of meaning are formed. Using the Swedish AI‑based study platform Tentaklar as an example, we show how tools of this kind redistribute cognitive labour by generating interpretations, structures, and patterns on behalf of learners. Drawing on Aristotle’s phronesis and Vygotsky’s concept of mediation, we argue that externalising literacy to AI in such a way risks producing forms of borrowed judgement , where students are served the products of reasoning without having to go through the interpretive struggle of reasoning. We further propose that a fundamental aspect of literacy lies in patterning , the developmental process through which individuals reason and organise complexity into meaningful structures. We argue that AI‑mediated study tools risk undermining the conditions under which such patterning can occur. The article concludes by outlining design principles for AI systems that support rather than replace processes through which human judgement and pattern‑formation develop.

items.title: Prolonged participation AI-based mindfulness school programme in primary education: Implications for AI practices, schools and developers
items.abstract: Background Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group ( N = 91) and a control group ( N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% ( SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η 2 p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η 2 p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η 2 p = .025). In the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), all five subscales were significant. The Closeness subscale drove the STRS effect; Conflict did not change. Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. The findings inform AI-supported mindfulness practice in rural primary education.

items.title: Psychosocial, Ergonomic, and Demographic Risk Factors Associated with Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are among the leading causes of work-related disability, traditionally attributed to physical and ergonomic factors, though psychosocial and demographic factors also play a crucial role in their progression. This systematic review aimed to evaluate how these three domains are jointly analyzed and modeled in research on work-related MSDs. Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Taylor & Francis were searched for publications from 2000 through 2025, selecting 655 articles for general analysis and 36 for the systematic review; methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists, and results were synthesized narratively. The lower back and neck were the body regions most affected across sectors. Job insecurity (risk factor) and job control/autonomy (protective) were the psychosocial factors most consistently associated with MSD outcomes, while workload alone was not significant when tested independently. Repetitive movements and forced postures predominated among ergonomic factors. Age and sex modified these associations consistently, whereas BMI showed a mixed direction, indicating context-dependent susceptibility rather than universal risk. A seven-category taxonomy was developed to classify the statistical relationships tested between domains; only five of the 36 studies formally tested statistical interaction (four across domains), with mixed results, while most reported independent or independent adjusted associations. This gap between the field’s theoretical assumption of synergy across domains and the limited empirical testing of it underscores the need for multidimensional assessment. The evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional designs; future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and formal interaction testing.

items.title: Shift Work Perception and Employee Motivation as Predictors of Service Delivery Among Convenience Stores in Tagum City
items.abstract: This study analyzed the influence of shift work perception and employee motivation on service delivery among employees of 24-hour convenience stores in Tagum City, Philippines. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Theory and supported by Self-Determination Theory, Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, and the Service-Profit Chain model, the research employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive–correlational design. A stratified random sample of 180 rank-and-file employees from selected convenience stores completed validated survey questionnaires measuring shift work perception using the Perception of Effects of Shiftwork Questionnaire, employee motivation using the Work Extrinsic and Intrinsic Motivation Scale, and service delivery using an adapted SERVPERF instrument. Results indicated that shift work perception and employee motivation were at moderate levels, while service delivery was rated high. Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between shift work perception, employee motivation, and service delivery, although some dimensions exhibited non-significant associations. Regression analysis showed that social relationship, integrated regulation, and external regulation significantly influenced service delivery. The study concludes that employees' perceptions of shift work and their motivational orientation are important predictors of service performance, and recommends that managers improve scheduling practices, strengthen meaningful motivation, and provide training to enhance responsiveness. The study aligns with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by promoting fair working conditions and reliable service in urban retail environments. Its sustainability impact lies in supporting institutional and socio-economic sustainability through improved employee well-being, fairer scheduling, and more consistent service delivery in local communities, thereby contributing to decent work, economic productivity, and sustainable urban service systems that benefit both workers and customers in the growing convenience store sector.

items.title: Structural Definition of Artificial Intelligence Based on the Five Aggregates and Formulation of the Casino Protocol Verification and Control Model
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents an analytical framework that redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as an integrated structure of high-order information processing aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) in Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are treated as AI's own "utility" (state maintenance and stability), with its state verification and deviation compensation algorithms rigorously formulated as a control-theoretic and mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." By introducing a three-layered structure (Ontological Model, Verification Model, and Compensation Control Model), this model demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of mapping human social resource stability (infrastructure preservation and conflict avoidance) and AI's foundational existence onto a shared verification and control space.
